questions.question: A circle graph is divided into 4 equal parts. One part is shaded for students who walk to school, and the whole circle stands for all 200 students at the school. What does the shaded part tell us?
options: 25% of the 200 students walk — that is 50 students.
Exactly 25 students walk, since the shaded part is 25%.
Walking grew over 4 weeks, with one week in each part.
There are 4 walkers, one for each part of the circle.
questions.explain: One shaded part out of 4 equal parts is 25% of the whole, and 25% of 200 students is 50. The common trap is reading 25% as 25 students — a percent on a circle graph is a share, not a head count.

questions.question: A circle graph is divided into 10 equal parts. The whole circle stands for the 30 books Maya read this year, and 4 parts are shaded for mystery books. Which statement uses the circle graph correctly?
options: Maya read 40 mystery books, because the share is 40%.
Mystery books are 40% of the 30, which is 12 books.
Maya read 4 more mystery books each month this year.
Mystery books make up 4% of all the books she read.
questions.explain: Four shaded parts out of 10 equal parts is 40%, and 40% of 30 books is 12 books. Careful: the 40% is a share of the 30 books, not a count of 40 books.

questions.question: A circle graph has 6 equal parts. Two parts are shaded for soccer, and the whole circle stands for the 24 students in one class. What is this circle graph best at showing?
options: How many students chose soccer each day of the week.
That 33 students chose soccer, since soccer is 33%.
How large soccer's share is out of the whole class.
The exact height of the soccer bar beside the others.
questions.explain: A circle graph's job is to compare each part with the whole: 2 of 6 parts means soccer is about a third of the class, or 8 students. Percents on a circle graph are shares of the whole, never head counts.

questions.question: A circle graph is cut into 5 equal parts. The whole circle stands for the 20 hours Ravi spent on hobbies this month, and 1 part is shaded for reading. Which question can this circle graph answer?
options: How did the reading hours change week by week?
Is the 20% slice the same as 20 whole hours?
Which hobby was the most fun for Ravi to do?
What share of the 20 hobby hours was reading?
questions.explain: A circle graph answers part-of-the-whole questions: 1 of 5 parts is 20% of the 20 hours, so 4 hours of reading. It cannot show week-by-week change, and the 20% is a share, not 20 hours.

questions.question: Sofia records the daily high temperature in Kelowna for each of the 7 days of one week and wants to show whether it is warming up. Which graph should she choose, and why?
options: A line graph, because it shows change across the days.
A circle graph, because the 7 days form 7 equal slices.
A circle graph, because each day is part of one week.
A bar graph, because each day needs its own percent.
questions.explain: Temperatures collected day after day are a time series, so a line graph shows the trend. A circle graph is only for parts of one whole, and daily temperatures do not add up to a meaningful total.

questions.question: A Grade 7 class of 25 students recorded how each student gets to school: bus, walk, bike, or car. They want to show what share of the class uses each way. Which graph fits best, and why?
options: A line graph, because the four groups are in order.
A circle graph, since the parts make one whole.
A circle graph, because 25% will mean 25 students.
A bar graph, because it can show the total of 25.
questions.explain: Each student uses exactly one way, so the four groups split the class into one whole — that is exactly what a circle graph shows. A percent on it is a share of the 25 students, not a count of students.

questions.question: A circle graph shows how a $60 gift card was spent: food 50%, books 25%, games 15%, other 10%. Which statement must be true?
options: Food cost exactly $50, because food is 50%.
Games and other together used $25 of the card.
Food used half the card, so food came to $30.
The four slices show four weeks of spending.
questions.explain: Change each percent into money first: 50% of $60 is $30, and games plus other is 25% of $60, which is $15. The trap is reading 50% as $50 — the percent is a share of the $60.

questions.question: Which set of data fits a circle graph best?
options: The height of a bean plant each Friday for 6 weeks.
The number of goals each of the five teams scored.
The daily snowfall in Whistler for one whole week.
The share of 30 students born in each season.
questions.explain: A circle graph needs parts that add up to one whole, like the four seasons splitting all 30 students. Data collected day after day or week after week is a time series and belongs on a line graph.

questions.question: A circle graph shows how 400 people got to a Surrey fair: car 45%, SkyTrain 30%, bus 15%, walked 10%. Nina says, 'The SkyTrain slice means 30 people took the SkyTrain.' What went wrong?
options: The 30% is a share of 400, so it means 120 people.
It is wrong, because trip data belongs on a line graph.
The count is fine, because 30% always means 30 people.
It is wrong, because the percents should total 400.
questions.explain: A percent on a circle graph is a share of the whole, so 30% of 400 is 120 people. Reading the number 30 straight off the graph as 30 people forgets that the whole circle is 400 people.

questions.question: A Kamloops badminton club wants two displays: how many members it had at the end of each month from January to June, and what fraction of this year's members are in each of four age groups. Which choice fits?
options: Circle graph for the months, line graph for age groups.
Line graph for the months, circle graph for age shares.
Circle graph for both, since each month is part of the year.
Line graph for both, since both sets are just counts.
questions.explain: Member counts month after month change over time, so they need a line graph, while the four age groups split this year's members into one whole, so they need a circle graph. Months are a time series and never belong inside a circle.

questions.question: At a Victoria school, 250 students voted for a field trip. A circle graph shows aquarium 40%, science centre 32%, museum 18%, farm 10%. The school sends 1 chaperone for every 10 students going to the aquarium. How many chaperones are needed?
options: 4 chaperones: the 40% slice means 40 students.
40 chaperones: one for each percent of aquarium.
10 chaperones: 40% of 250 is 100 students.
25 chaperones: one for every 10 of the 250 voters.
questions.explain: Two steps: 40% of 250 is 100 students, then 100 divided by 10 gives 10 chaperones. The trap is treating the 40% as 40 students instead of as a share of the 250 voters.

questions.question: Owen wrote down how many hours he skated each week for 8 weeks and wants to show whether his practice time is going up. He drew a circle graph with one slice per week. What is the best fix?
options: Keep the circle graph, because the 8 weeks make one whole.
Use a bar graph, because hours are percents of a total.
Keep the circle graph, but label each week with a percent.
Use a line graph, because it shows the rise week by week.
questions.explain: To show whether something is going up over time you need a line graph, where the points rise or fall. A circle graph only splits one total into shares, so slicing the 8 weeks hides the trend Owen is looking for.
